name: Philippines (since 1946)
summary: The Republic of the Philippines, independent from the United States since 1946: an archipelago of about 7,641 islands with over 114 million people.

location.value: An archipelago in the western Pacific: Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao; about 7,641 islands.

terrain.value: More than 7,000 islands, many volcanic and mountainous, with narrow coastal plains.
terrain.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

climate.value: Tropical and humid, with a rainy season and about 20 typhoons a year.
climate.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

resources.value: Rice and coconut farmland, nickel, copper and gold, large fisheries and coral reefs.
resources.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

disasters.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

population.value: More than 110 million people (2020 census: about 109 million); one of the fastest-growing in Asia.

urbanisation.value: About half the people live in towns and cities; Metro Manila has over 13 million.
urbanisation.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

disease.value: Dengue fever, tuberculosis, and COVID-19 (with one of Asia’s longest lockdowns, 2020–21).
disease.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

migration.value: Millions work abroad as overseas Filipino workers.
migration.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

economicBase.value: Services (including call centres), money sent home by overseas workers, electronics exports and farming.
economicBase.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

tradeRoutes.value: Trades mostly with the United States, Japan, China and other Asian countries.
tradeRoutes.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income economy with fast growth since the 2010s.
wealth.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

moneyAndTax.value: The Philippine peso; income tax and VAT.
moneyAndTax.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

inequality.value: High inequality; a few wealthy families own much of the land and business.
inequality.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

governmentType.value: A presidential republic, with a president elected for one six-year term.
governmentType.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

keyRulers.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

succession.value: Presidential elections every six years; martial law under Marcos (1972–81) suspended them.
succession.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

institutions.value: The 1987 constitution, written after the fall of Marcos, with Congress and a Supreme Court.
institutions.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

stability.value: Martial law (1972–81); the People Power Revolution (1986).
stability.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

eliteConflict.value: Powerful political families (“dynasties”) compete for national and local office.
eliteConflict.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

armyAndTech.value: The Armed Forces of the Philippines; a mutual defence treaty with the United States (1951).
armyAndTech.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

majorWars.value: The Hukbalahap rebellion (1946–54); communist and Moro insurgencies; the Battle of Marawi (2017).
majorWars.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

territoryChange.value: Disputes with China over islands in the South China Sea; an international tribunal ruled for the Philippines in 2016.
territoryChange.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with the United States; a founding member of ASEAN (1967).
alliancesRivals.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

inventions.value: Roberto del Rosario patented a karaoke “Sing-Along System” in the Philippines (1975); Japan’s Daisuke Inoue is more widely credited with karaoke.
inventions.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

scienceEducation.value: High literacy; English is widely used in schools and universities.
scienceEducation.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

openness.value: Strong US influence and a large share of workers abroad.
openness.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

religion.value: Mostly Catholic (about 80%); a Muslim minority mainly in Mindanao.
religion.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

languageWriting.value: Filipino (based on Tagalog) and English are official; more than 170 languages are spoken.
languageWriting.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

artsArchitecture.value: Baroque churches of the Philippines (a World Heritage Site), jeepney decoration and modern film.
artsArchitecture.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

socialStructure.value: Large gaps between rich and poor; a growing urban middle class.
socialStructure.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

sharedIdentity.value: A Filipino identity shaped by Spanish, American and Asian influences and by heroes such as José Rizal.
sharedIdentity.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

neighbours.value: Taiwan, Japan, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, China (maritime).
neighbours.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

ideasReligions.value: Catholicism and democratic ideals; the 1986 People Power Revolution inspired others.
ideasReligions.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

colonisation.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

riseSignals.value: Independence from the United States on 4 July 1946.

peakPeriod.value: Still exists; strong growth in the 2010s.
peakPeriod.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

declineSignals.value: Not applicable: still exists. Challenges include inequality, insurgency and typhoons.
declineSignals.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)

outcome.value: Continues today as the Republic of the Philippines.
outcome.source: Abinales & Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2017)
